name: Feminist theory
summary: Feminist theory is the extension of feminism into theoretical and philosophical discourse: the study of how gender inequality arises and works, in political thought, ethics, epistemology, economics and other fields. Its scholars hold that women have been systematically subordinated, that gender is largely socially shaped, and that analysis should serve changing the world, while they disagree widely on sex work, pornography, the category of "woman" and the economic system.

notFound.work: Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (full text)

tried.how: searched for an open-access copy of the text

scope: Feminist theory as scholarship describes it: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entries on feminist political philosophy, sex and gender, the history of feminist thought, class and work, ethics, epistemology and topics in feminism. The texts those entries treat as canonical (Wollstonecraft's Vindication, Mill's Subjection of Women, the Combahee statement as the intersectional strand) answer where they state a position. Where strands of the theory differ and no source takes a side, the answer is null. Movements and individual theorists' own programmes are other subjects.

notes: Themes searched in the Stanford entries without finding a position held by feminist theory as a whole: economy and markets, taxation, welfare, government and constitutions, the military and war, immigration, ecology, technology, speech and pornography (MacKinnon's case for restriction is one strand), religion, same-sex marriage, quotas and parity, and foreign policy. The entries say there is little consensus among feminist theorists on most questions, so those answers are null. Sex work is a documented split (0, low). Beauvoir's The Second Sex and Butler's works were not available as open full text. The uncertainty rule may fail because the record says little on economic, constitutional and foreign-policy lines; that is an honest result.
